subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] The Principal Appellant (XXXX XXXX), his wife, the Associate Appellant (XXXX XXXX) and their children, the minor Appellants (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX), are all citizens of India.

[2] The Appellants allege that they cannot return to India because the Principal Appellant is a member of the Indian National Lok Dal (INLD) party in Karnal, Haryana. The Principal Appellant alleges that Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Chief Minister (CM) of Haryana, pressured him to stop campaigning for the INLD and to instead join the BJP (Bharatiya Janata Party). When the Principal Appellant refused, he alleges that both the BJP and the RSS (Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh) harassed him and targeted his business (a XXXX XXXX) to hurt him financially.

[3] The Principal Appellant also alleges that in June 2018, he launched a protest against the BJP government and, along with 3 other INLD party members, was arrested, kidnapped and tortured at an abandoned rice mill for two days and was told that he must apologize to the Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar and join the BJP.

[4] The Appellants came to Canada on visitor visas in 2017 and stayed for 20 to 25 days.1 The Principal Appellant travelled to Canada a second time, alone, in XXXX 2018. He stayed with friends and accompanied them on a one-week trip to the United States; from there he returned to Canada.2 The Associate Appellant and minor Appellants joined the Principal Appellant in Canada in XXXX 2018. The Appellants then applied for refugee protection together on November 29, 2018.

[5] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) determined that some of the Appellants' allegations lacked credibility. The RPD also reasoned, a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) exists in Kolkata, West Bengal.

[6] The Appellants submit that the RPD ignored the country condition evidence and that the RPD erred in finding that a viable IFA exists.

[7] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3
DECISION

[8] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

[9] The RPD was correct in rejecting their claim due to both the lack of credibility of the allegations, as well as the viability of the proposed IFA.
NEW EVIDENCE

[10] The Appellants have presented no new evidence with their appeal record and both the Principal Appellant and the Associate Appellant stipulated in their declarations that they are not seeking to introduce any new evidence.4 I therefore conclude, that the statement in their Memorandum which refers to 'new developments' was included in error - in the Memorandum it states: "the Applicant likewise relies on the facts set out in his personal Affidavit sworn on date 2020, August 18, and new developments, exhibits attached thereto."5

ANALYSIS

[11] I have attentively listened to the recording of the RPD hearing, and have carefully reviewed the entire record. I agree with the RPD's decision.
The Appellants' Memorandum

[12] In their Memorandum, the Appellants advance two arguments: (1) that the RPD failed to take into account the strength of the BJP and RSS organisations and (2) that the RPD failed to consider the objective documentation on the ability of the state to track individuals throughout the country. I will address both of these arguments later in these reasons.

[13] First of all, it is important to note that the Appellants have not contested the credibility findings made by the RPD. These are the following:
a. The RPD concluded that the Principal Appellant's allegation that, while he was hiding at his sister's house in New Delhi in July 2018, it was raided by Haryana police, at the behest of the RSS in order to locate him, was not credible. The reasons for this finding are set out in paragraphs 12-14 of the RPD's reasons. I agree with the RPD's reasons and also find this allegation not to be credible.
b. The RPD gave no weight to the affidavits written by his friend (XXXX XXXX), the Principal Appellant's mother (XXXX XXXX XXXXand brother (XXXX XXXX) for the reasons set out in paragraphs 15 to 18 of the RPD's reasons. I agree with the RPD that these affidavits should not be given any weight.
c. The RPD concluded that the Principal Appellant's allegation that he was accused of cow smuggling and other fraudulent criminal charges by the Haryana police, was not credible for the reasons set out in paragraphs 19 to 22 of the RPD's reasons. I agree with the RPD that these allegations are not credible.

subthemes.text:
[14] Therefore, the RPD appears to have found only the following allegations to be credible:
a. The Principal Appellant was a member of the INLD.
b. The Principal Appellant was harassed by the Chief Minister of Haryana (XXXX XXXX XXXX) who attempted to convince him to abandon his party and join the BJP instead. This harassment involved attempts to disrupt his supply of gas and diesel for the Principal Appellant's XXXX XXXX. It also involved complaints against the gas station, notices from the pollution board and an eviction notice from the National Highway Authority. However, the Principal Appellant testified that he was ultimately able to rectify these matters because he had all the proper permissions.6
c. After protesting against the BJP in late June 2018, the Principal Appellant, along with three other INLD party members were arrested and told to apologize to the Chief Minister.

[15] I agree with the RPD that the above allegations, on a balance of probabilities, are credible.

[16] The RPD reasoned that the Appellants would nevertheless be safe in Kolkata, West Bengal, where the BJP is not in power. I agree with the RPD on this point. Given that the BJP is not in power in Kolkata, it would be reasonable to assume that the Principal Appellant would be able to freely espouse his political views without interference from the BJP.

[17] The RPD also noted that the country condition documentation suggests that, due to limited interstate police communication as well as the limits of the criminal tracking systems and central monitoring systems, it would be unlikely that Haryana police would be able to locate the Appellants in West Bengal. In conducting my independent assessment, I do not find the lack, if any, of connectivity between police services across India to be important to this case.

[18] As pointed out by the RPD, far more important in my view, is the fact that that Principal Appellant has never been formally charged with any crime in India, there is no evidence his name is on a list of wanted individuals and no First Information Report or warrant has been issued against him. Furthermore, I note that the adult Appellants both testified that they had no difficulty leaving the country using their own genuine passports.7 Therefore, there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Principal Appellant's name would be registered in any criminal tracking database or on any sort of watch-list database which would be searched during the tenant verification system.

[19] In terms of motivation of the alleged persecutors, I also note that the Principal Appellant's XXXX XXXX business continues to be in operation, and while the Principal Appellant asserts that people come around asking for him at the XXXX XXXX, and informing his employees that they will exact their revenge8, the fact remains that the gas station itself is still able to operate 'very successfully' according to the Principal Appellant.9 I note that, as the XXXX XXXX was the target of the BJP in the past in order to put financial pressure on the Appellant to leave the INLD, it stands to reason that the fact that his XXXX XXXX continues to operate at this time, unhindered, is evidence of a waning interest in the Principal Appellant - particularly given his absence from Karnal, Haryana.

[20] Therefore, I agree with the RPD that Kolkata satisfies the first prong of the IFA test. I also agree with the RPD's reasoning on the second prong of the test, set out at paragraphs 29 to 34 of its reasons.
The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to appreciate the strength of the BJP and RSS

[21] In their Memorandum, the Appellants submit: "the honourable member did not take into consideration he capabilities of BJP and RSS cadre and its strength while proposing Kolkata as IFA. Haryana police which is under the direct influence of the BJP and RSS as they govern the state can do anything to please their political masters. As police in India shares information with each other and there are many pan India integrated police software system's which are being used by the security agencies and state police to track individuals in other states."10

[22] The Appellants cite the January 31, 2020 version of the National Documentation package (NDP) item 4.6 which, according to the Appellants, shows that "in the last general elections which was held in India in March to May 2019. BJP won 18 parliamentary seats out of total 42 parliamentary seats in state of West Bengal. BJP had got 42.86% of the total vote share in this state. This clearly shows that BJP has a strong base in this state."11

[23] While the Appellants are correct that the BJP won 18 out of 42 seats in West Bengal in 2019, the RPD was nevertheless correct in stating that the BJP is not in power. It is the AITC party which remains in power in West Bengal. (The All India Trinamool Congress)12 The RPD did not, therefore, err in concluding that, given the Principal Appellant's political views against the BJP, he would be safe from harassment or mistreatment, on a balance of probabilities, in West Bengal where the BJP does not enjoy the support of the majority.

[24] I am therefore satisfied that the RPD did not err and did not misjudge the country condition documentation on the strength of either the BJP or the RSS when it determined that Kolkata is a viable IFA.
The Appellants submit the RPD failed to consider the objective documentation on the ability of the state to track individuals

[25] The Appellants submit that they would not be safe anywhere in India as the BJP and RSS will be able to track them anywhere in the country using the state's apparatus for tracking criminals. The Appellants cite item 10.6 of the NDP - Surveillance by state authorities; communication between police offices across the country and the use of the CCTNS.13

[26] As explained earlier in this decision, the RPD correctly concluded that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Principal Appellant's name would be on any government list or included in a database used to track criminals or on any sort of watch list database which would be searched during the tenant verification system. Therefore, I am satisfied that, technological advancements in connectivity aside, the RPD was correct to conclude that these verification systems do not signify that Haryana police would search for and find the Appellants, should they relocate to Kolkata.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] The Principal Appellant (XXXX XXXX), his wife, the Associate Appellant (XXXX XXXX) and their children, the minor Appellants (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX), are all citizens of India.

[2] The Appellants allege that they cannot return to India because the Principal Appellant is a member of the Indian National Lok Dal (INLD) party in Karnal, Haryana. The Principal Appellant alleges that Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Chief Minister (CM) of Haryana, pressured him to stop campaigning for the INLD and to instead join the BJP (Bharatiya Janata Party). When the Principal Appellant refused, he alleges that both the BJP and the RSS (Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh) harassed him and targeted his business (a XXXX XXXX) to hurt him financially.

[3] The Principal Appellant also alleges that in June 2018, he launched a protest against the BJP government and, along with 3 other INLD party members, was arrested, kidnapped and tortured at an abandoned rice mill for two days and was told that he must apologize to the Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar and join the BJP.

[4] The Appellants came to Canada on visitor visas in 2017 and stayed for 20 to 25 days.1 The Principal Appellant travelled to Canada a second time, alone, in XXXX 2018. He stayed with friends and accompanied them on a one-week trip to the United States; from there he returned to Canada.2 The Associate Appellant and minor Appellants joined the Principal Appellant in Canada in XXXX 2018. The Appellants then applied for refugee protection together on November 29, 2018.

[5] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) determined that some of the Appellants' allegations lacked credibility. The RPD also reasoned, a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) exists in Kolkata, West Bengal.
[6] The Appellants submit that the RPD ignored the country condition evidence and that the RPD erred in finding that a viable IFA exists.

[7] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3
DECISION
[8] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

[9] The RPD was correct in rejecting their claim due to both the lack of credibility of the allegations, as well as the viability of the proposed IFA.
NEW EVIDENCE

[10] The Appellants have presented no new evidence with their appeal record and both the Principal Appellant and the Associate Appellant stipulated in their declarations that they are not seeking to introduce any new evidence.4 I therefore conclude, that the statement in their Memorandum which refers to 'new developments' was included in error - in the Memorandum it states: "the Applicant likewise relies on the facts set out in his personal Affidavit sworn on date 2020, August 18, and new developments, exhibits attached thereto."5
ANALYSIS

[11] I have attentively listened to the recording of the RPD hearing, and have carefully reviewed the entire record. I agree with the RPD's decision.
The Appellants' Memorandum

[12] In their Memorandum, the Appellants advance two arguments: (1) that the RPD failed to take into account the strength of the BJP and RSS organisations and (2) that the RPD failed to consider the objective documentation on the ability of the state to track individuals throughout the country. I will address both of these arguments later in these reasons.

[13] First of all, it is important to note that the Appellants have not contested the credibility findings made by the RPD. These are the following:
a. The RPD concluded that the Principal Appellant's allegation that, while he was hiding at his sister's house in New Delhi in July 2018, it was raided by Haryana police, at the behest of the RSS in order to locate him, was not credible. The reasons for this finding are set out in paragraphs 12-14 of the RPD's reasons. I agree with the RPD's reasons and also find this allegation not to be credible.
b. The RPD gave no weight to the affidavits written by his friend (XXXX XXXX), the Principal Appellant's mother (XXXX XXXX XXXXand brother (XXXX XXXX) for the reasons set out in paragraphs 15 to 18 of the RPD's reasons. I agree with the RPD that these affidavits should not be given any weight.
c. The RPD concluded that the Principal Appellant's allegation that he was accused of cow smuggling and other fraudulent criminal charges by the Haryana police, was not credible for the reasons set out in paragraphs 19 to 22 of the RPD's reasons. I agree with the RPD that these allegations are not credible.

[14] Therefore, the RPD appears to have found only the following allegations to be credible:
a. The Principal Appellant was a member of the INLD.
b. The Principal Appellant was harassed by the Chief Minister of Haryana (XXXX XXXX XXXX) who attempted to convince him to abandon his party and join the BJP instead. This harassment involved attempts to disrupt his supply of gas and diesel for the Principal Appellant's XXXX XXXX. It also involved complaints against the gas station, notices from the pollution board and an eviction notice from the National Highway Authority. However, the Principal Appellant testified that he was ultimately able to rectify these matters because he had all the proper permissions.6
c. After protesting against the BJP in late June 2018, the Principal Appellant, along with three other INLD party members were arrested and told to apologize to the Chief Minister.
[15] I agree with the RPD that the above allegations, on a balance of probabilities, are credible.

[16] The RPD reasoned that the Appellants would nevertheless be safe in Kolkata, West Bengal, where the BJP is not in power. I agree with the RPD on this point. Given that the BJP is not in power in Kolkata, it would be reasonable to assume that the Principal Appellant would be able to freely espouse his political views without interference from the BJP.

[17] The RPD also noted that the country condition documentation suggests that, due to limited interstate police communication as well as the limits of the criminal tracking systems and central monitoring systems, it would be unlikely that Haryana police would be able to locate the Appellants in West Bengal. In conducting my independent assessment, I do not find the lack, if any, of connectivity between police services across India to be important to this case.

[18] As pointed out by the RPD, far more important in my view, is the fact that that Principal Appellant has never been formally charged with any crime in India, there is no evidence his name is on a list of wanted individuals and no First Information Report or warrant has been issued against him. Furthermore, I note that the adult Appellants both testified that they had no difficulty leaving the country using their own genuine passports.7 Therefore, there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Principal Appellant's name would be registered in any criminal tracking database or on any sort of watch-list database which would be searched during the tenant verification system.

[19] In terms of motivation of the alleged persecutors, I also note that the Principal Appellant's XXXX XXXX business continues to be in operation, and while the Principal Appellant asserts that people come around asking for him at the XXXX XXXX, and informing his employees that they will exact their revenge8, the fact remains that the gas station itself is still able to operate 'very successfully' according to the Principal Appellant.9 I note that, as the XXXX XXXX was the target of the BJP in the past in order to put financial pressure on the Appellant to leave the INLD, it stands to reason that the fact that his XXXX XXXX continues to operate at this time, unhindered, is evidence of a waning interest in the Principal Appellant - particularly given his absence from Karnal, Haryana.

[20] Therefore, I agree with the RPD that Kolkata satisfies the first prong of the IFA test. I also agree with the RPD's reasoning on the second prong of the test, set out at paragraphs 29 to 34 of its reasons.
The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to appreciate the strength of the BJP and RSS

[21] In their Memorandum, the Appellants submit: "the honourable member did not take into consideration he capabilities of BJP and RSS cadre and its strength while proposing Kolkata as IFA. Haryana police which is under the direct influence of the BJP and RSS as they govern the state can do anything to please their political masters. As police in India shares information with each other and there are many pan India integrated police software system's which are being used by the security agencies and state police to track individuals in other states."10

[22] The Appellants cite the January 31, 2020 version of the National Documentation package (NDP) item 4.6 which, according to the Appellants, shows that "in the last general elections which was held in India in March to May 2019. BJP won 18 parliamentary seats out of total 42 parliamentary seats in state of West Bengal. BJP had got 42.86% of the total vote share in this state. This clearly shows that BJP has a strong base in this state."11

[23] While the Appellants are correct that the BJP won 18 out of 42 seats in West Bengal in 2019, the RPD was nevertheless correct in stating that the BJP is not in power. It is the AITC party which remains in power in West Bengal. (The All India Trinamool Congress)12 The RPD did not, therefore, err in concluding that, given the Principal Appellant's political views against the BJP, he would be safe from harassment or mistreatment, on a balance of probabilities, in West Bengal where the BJP does not enjoy the support of the majority.

[24] I am therefore satisfied that the RPD did not err and did not misjudge the country condition documentation on the strength of either the BJP or the RSS when it determined that Kolkata is a viable IFA.
The Appellants submit the RPD failed to consider the objective documentation on the ability of the state to track individuals

[25] The Appellants submit that they would not be safe anywhere in India as the BJP and RSS will be able to track them anywhere in the country using the state's apparatus for tracking criminals. The Appellants cite item 10.6 of the NDP - Surveillance by state authorities; communication between police offices across the country and the use of the CCTNS.13

[26] As explained earlier in this decision, the RPD correctly concluded that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Principal Appellant's name would be on any government list or included in a database used to track criminals or on any sort of watch list database which would be searched during the tenant verification system. Therefore, I am satisfied that, technological advancements in connectivity aside, the RPD was correct to conclude that these verification systems do not signify that Haryana police would search for and find the Appellants, should they relocate to Kolkata.
CONCLUSION

[27] I am not satisfied the Appellants have demonstrated that there is a serious possibility that they would be persecuted if they returned to India, specifically to the IFA city proposed (Kolkata), nor that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should they return to India, specifically to Kolkata.
(signed)
Jillan Sadek
Jillan Sadek
February 8, 2021
